title: Chest pain and ST elevation in every lead
presentation: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with two days of sharp retrosternal chest pain that is worse lying flat and on inspiration, and eases when he sits forward. Triage: HR 98, BP 124/78, T 37.9 C, SpO2 98% on air. The triage ECG shows ST elevation in leads I, II, aVL, aVF and V2-V6, and the cath lab has been put on standby.

stages.label: History
stages.text: He had a sore throat, myalgias and a low-grade fever ten days ago that settled on their own. The pain radiates to the top of his left shoulder (the trapezius ridge) and is not exertional. No dyspnoea at rest, no syncope, no palpitations. He is a non-smoker, does not use cocaine or other stimulants, has no diabetes or hypertension, and has no family history of premature coronary disease or sudden death. No recent travel, no tuberculosis contacts, no known autoimmune disease, no recent chest trauma or cardiac procedure. Medications: none. He has not yet taken any anti-inflammatory.
stages.prompt: What is your differential for this ECG, and does he belong in the cath lab right now? Tell me what on the ECG would push you either way.
stages.learner_goal: Hold STEMI and pericarditis side by side and name the ECG features that discriminate between them, rather than anchoring on the ST elevation alone.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: HR 96 regular, BP 122/76 in both arms, pulsus paradoxus 6 mmHg, afebrile now. JVP not elevated. Heart sounds: a scratchy, triphasic rub at the left lower sternal border, loudest with the patient leaning forward in held expiration. Lungs clear. No peripheral oedema. Radial and femoral pulses equal and symmetric. No calf swelling or tenderness.
stages.prompt: Commit to your leading diagnosis. Which tests do you want to confirm it, and which do you want to be sure you are not missing something dangerous?
stages.learner_goal: Recognise the rub, check for tamponade physiology, and order troponin, echo and inflammatory markers.

available_tests.ecg: Repeat 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm 96. Concave ('saddle-shaped') ST elevation of 1-2 mm in I, II, III, aVL, aVF and V2-V6, not confined to a single coronary territory. PR-segment depression in II, aVF and V4-V6 with PR elevation in aVR. ST depression in aVR and V1 only; no reciprocal ST depression elsewhere. ST elevation to T-wave amplitude ratio in V6 is 0.33. No Q waves.
available_tests.troponin: High-sensitivity troponin I 18 ng/L at presentation (upper reference limit 34) and 21 ng/L at 3 hours.
available_tests.echocardiogram: Bedside echo: trivial posterior pericardial effusion (4 mm). Normal left ventricular size and systolic function, no regional wall motion abnormality, no right atrial or right ventricular collapse, inferior vena cava 1.6 cm with normal respiratory collapse.
available_tests.cbc: WBC 10.2 x10^9/L (lymphocyte predominant), Hb 14.6 g/dL, platelets 260.
available_tests.chest x-ray: Normal cardiac silhouette, normal mediastinal width, clear lung fields.

stages.label: Labs
stages.text: Repeat ECG shows concave ST elevation across inferior, lateral and anterior leads with PR depression, PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal ST depression apart from aVR and V1. Troponin 18 ng/L then 21 ng/L at three hours. Bedside echo: 4 mm pericardial effusion, normal LV function, no wall motion abnormality, no chamber collapse. CRP 68 mg/L, ESR 42. Chest radiograph normal. Pain unchanged.
stages.prompt: Put it together. What is the diagnosis, how do you treat him, and does he need to be admitted?
stages.learner_goal: Name acute pericarditis, prescribe an NSAID with colchicine, and apply the high-risk criteria to decide disposition.

key_clues: Pleuritic, positional chest pain radiating to the trapezius ridge after a viral prodrome
ST elevation across multiple coronary territories with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR and V1
Concave ST morphology and ST/T ratio in V6 above 0.25
Flat, normal serial troponin with no regional wall motion abnormality on echo

distractors.name: ST-elevation myocardial infarction
distractors.why_not: ST elevation spans inferior, lateral and anterior leads rather than one coronary territory, is concave, has no reciprocal depression, is accompanied by PR depression, and serial troponin is normal with no wall motion abnormality. Had any of those pointed the other way, he would have gone to the cath lab.

distractors.name: Myocarditis or myopericarditis
distractors.why_not: Troponin is normal on two draws and LV function is preserved.

distractors.name: Cardiac tamponade
distractors.why_not: Pulsus paradoxus 6 mmHg, JVP normal, effusion is 4 mm with no chamber collapse.

distractors.name: Aortic dissection
distractors.why_not: Pain is pleuritic and positional rather than tearing; blood pressures and pulses are symmetric; mediastinum is normal on the radiograph.

distractors.name: Pulmonary embolism
distractors.why_not: No hypoxia, heart rate under 100, no risk factors, negative D-dimer, and the ECG is not a right heart strain pattern.

distractors.name: Benign early repolarisation
distractors.why_not: Early repolarisation does not produce PR depression, a rub, fever or a raised CRP, and the ST/T ratio in V6 is above 0.25.

rubric.description: Names pericarditis in the initial differential
rubric.concept: Positional pleuritic chest pain with diffuse ST elevation is pericarditis until proven otherwise

rubric.description: Keeps STEMI or acute coronary occlusion actively on the table and says what would send him to the cath lab
rubric.concept: Diffuse ST elevation is pericarditis only after STEMI has been actively considered and excluded

rubric.description: Cites at least one discriminating ECG feature: non-territorial distribution, absent reciprocal change, concave morphology, PR depression, aVR changes or ST/T ratio
rubric.concept: ECG discriminators between pericarditis and STEMI: territory, reciprocal change, morphology, PR segment

rubric.description: Orders serial troponin to exclude infarction and myocardial involvement
rubric.concept: Troponin separates pericarditis from myopericarditis and infarction

rubric.description: Orders a bedside echo to look for effusion, tamponade and wall motion abnormality
rubric.concept: Echo in suspected pericarditis: effusion size, tamponade physiology, regional wall motion

rubric.description: Sends CRP or ESR to support the diagnosis and track response
rubric.concept: CRP supports the diagnosis of pericarditis and guides duration of therapy
Diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis: two of pain, rub, ECG changes, effusion

rubric.description: Prescribes a high-dose NSAID or aspirin plus colchicine
rubric.concept: NSAID plus colchicine is first-line for acute pericarditis; colchicine halves recurrence

rubric.description: Applies high-risk features to disposition, restricts exercise, and avoids corticosteroids as first-line
rubric.concept: High-risk features for pericarditis mandate admission; steroids increase recurrence; exercise restriction until CRP normal

management_summary: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily (or aspirin 750-1000 mg three times daily) for one to two weeks with a taper once pain-free and CRP normal, plus colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily (once daily if under 70 kg) for three months, with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection. No corticosteroids. Restrict exercise until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises. He has no high-risk features (temperature under 38 C, acute onset, effusion under 20 mm, no tamponade, no myocardial involvement, not immunosuppressed or anticoagulated, no trauma), so he can be discharged with review and a repeat CRP in one week.
teaching_points: Four ECG questions separate pericarditis from STEMI: does the elevation respect a coronary territory, is there reciprocal depression (other than aVR and V1), is the morphology concave or convex, and is there PR depression. None is perfect alone; a territorial or convex pattern, reciprocal change, or a rising troponin means the cath lab or a cardiology discussion within minutes.
Acute pericarditis needs two of four: characteristic pain, rub, typical ECG changes, and new or worsening effusion. CRP supports the diagnosis and tracks response.
NSAID plus colchicine is the standard of care; colchicine roughly halves recurrence (ICAP). Corticosteroids are second line because they increase recurrence.

High-risk features (fever over 38 C, subacute onset, large effusion or tamponade, failure to respond within a week, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, trauma, myopericarditis) mandate admission and a search for a cause; without them, outpatient treatment is safe.
references: Adler Y et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921-64
Imazio M et al. A randomized trial of colchicine for acute pericarditis (ICAP). N Engl J Med 2013;369:1522-8
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21e, Pericardial Disease
